---
name: testing
description: "How work is tested: test kinds and suites, test objects, how thoroughly a wrapper is tested, UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, equivalence and unit tests, and the C tests carried over; testing-builds and testing-gates give the builds, coverage and gates. Read before writing tests."
---

# Testing

Tests are classified by what decides them and by the side of a module they test, and each
is placed where the conventions' Testing section places tests of its kind:

- UB tests on the safe public interface show that it does not reach UB, mainly by not
  triggering sanitizer or Miri crashes, or by failing to compile for a given illegal path;
- UB tests on the unsafe public interface target UB there: each public `unsafe fn` or
  method a workset adds, called within its stated `# Safety` contract, edge cases
  included. Raw `sys::` round-trips are not UB tests on the unsafe interface; they are unit
  or equivalence tests;
- equivalence tests show that the Rust behaves as the C it translates, mainly by passing
  equivalence assertions: `equiv_pub` on the module's exported API, `equiv_priv` on its
  internals; and
- unit tests show that the Rust keeps its contract, by passing Rust assertions, without
  the C: `unit_pub` on the public interface, `unit_priv` on the internal routines.

<!-- TODO: fuzzing, of the safe public interface and differentially against the C, is
deferred. -->

Test objects are constructed through safe constructors. The UB tests on the safe public
interface use the safe API alone, their suite forbidding `unsafe_code` at its root: a type
that no safe constructor or producer yields yet gets those tests in the batch that wraps
its first one. Elsewhere, while a type has no safe constructor, one documented unsafe
fixture per type adopts the raw constructor's result, and is replaced once the safe
constructor exists.

A test exercises the safe API wherever it can, so that the later stages of a port, which
keep that API, keep it passing. A test of a C form an item keeps, such as an unsafe
adoption, a function pointer's unsafe constructor, a trampoline or an export, goes with
the stage that removes the form.

How thoroughly a wrapper is tested follows how long it lasts. One a port will replace, a
type wrapped ahead of its port or a dependency whose module will be ported, keeps its safe
API through the port: it gets the tests of its public interface, which outlive it, and
none of its internals. A permanent one, every wrapper of a wrap campaign, the foundational
modules' and one whose later stage is held back for good, gets every kind.

The builds the tests run against and how coverage is measured are
[`testing-builds`](builds/SKILL.md)'s, and the gates every landing passes
[`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. UB tests

UB tests show that a workset's public API is free of UB.

The unsafe public interface is tested with one suite per public unsafe function or method
a workset adds, its inputs built through the safe API wherever one exists. A workset that
adds no public unsafe API has no UB tests on the unsafe interface.

The sanitizers available are those the campaign built: the instrumented variants of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`, where `asan-ubsan` provides ASan and UBSan, `msan` MSan, `tsan` TSan
and `bsan` BSan. A sanitizer without a variant is not available, so no test is written for
it and none runs under it. Miri needs no C build and is always available.

A target that ships its own sanitizers, because the standard ones cannot run against it,
is tested with those instead, each standing for the sanitizer it implements.

Each available sanitizer is a separate obligation of an item while it reaches C or unsafe
code; once it reaches neither, as a port's later stages bring about, Miri covers it alone:

- ASan/UBSan: bounds errors, use-after-free, use-after-return, invalid free, double free,
  pointer/alignment UB, and integer/division/shift UB.
- MSan: use of uninitialized memory, including branches and addresses computed from it,
  uninitialized bytes crossing the FFI boundary, and struct tails or buffers a foreign
  initializer left partly unwritten. Its build instruments every component, the standard
  library through `-Zbuild-std` included: memory written by uninstrumented code reads as
  uninitialized, so a partial build reports falsely.
- BSan: conflicting foreign writes and retained foreign pointers across Rust reborrows.
  These tests are written like the others. BSan is the slowest instrument and reports
  false positives at the foreign boundary, so it runs only as
  [`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions section describes.
- TSan: races reachable through safe APIs, including every asserted `Send` or `Sync`
  implementation and threaded callback.
- Miri: Rust-side lifetime, bounds, initialization, validity, alignment, intrinsic, and
  `repr` assumptions. Miri cannot call the foreign library, read its globals or spawn a
  process, so every test that cannot run under it carries
  `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore = "<reason>")]` on its test function, naming what stops it:
  `"calls C"`, `"reads a C global"`, and so on. A test is marked only after it was run
  alone under Miri and seen to stop there; never to silence a Miri report of undefined
  behaviour, a panic or a failed assertion, which are findings. The mark goes once what it
  names no longer stops the test, as a module's switch or a later stage brings about. Neither
  `#[cfg(not(miri))]` nor test-name filters stand in for the attribute: with it in place,
  Miri runs every other test.

A leak is not undefined behaviour, in Rust or in C, so neither a LeakSanitizer report,
which ASan's runtime makes by default, nor Miri's leak check is a UB candidate.

UB tests exercise every owner and borrowed form, shared and mutable access path, lifecycle
strategy, generic instance, and callback variant a batch emits. They attempt to outlive the
owner, alias a reborrow, reenter a callback, and drop a parent first. Storage that C and
Rust both allocate or free, or whose allocator a port moves, is tested for a free through
the wrong allocator.

When the type system should reject a program, the test is a compile-fail doctest or a
`trybuild` case.

## 2. Equivalence tests

Equivalence tests run the C and the Rust that translates it on independently owned inputs
built from one description, and compare:

- return values and errors;
- out-parameters and buffers;
- callbacks;
- state transitions; and
- lifecycle effects.

They use multi-call sequences and compare after each step; single calls are only a
baseline.

The C side of a test meets the preconditions the C sets its callers, as the wrapper meets
them before its own calls: a library's global initialisation, which writes state its
routines read without synchronisation, runs before the test's first call that reads it,
since the harness runs other tests beside it on other threads.

They compare what the C specifies, through the mapping the safe API applies to it, such as
its status returns as errors and its null pointers as absent values, and not what it leaves
unspecified, such as an iteration order, a message's text, a pointer's value or an
allocation count. A confirmed C defect is not copied into Rust. The divergence is
documented, equivalence tests are retained for the unaffected behaviour, and the
corrected-behaviour regression is a unit test.

internal routine with its C counterpart only where one exists, since an idiomatic port may
restructure the internals; a C function the raw bindings do not reach, one with internal
linkage, is compared through the functions that call it. A macro that implements
logic is compared where it expands, through the functions that hold its expansions, since a
test of their callers compares the callers' logic, not the macro's. When no function the
raw bindings reach runs any of its expansions, directly or through the functions it calls,
no equivalence test compares it: its unit tests check it against the replacement list at
each expansion site's arguments, and the batch reports the sites as unreached, until the

- deliberate correction of defective C behaviour;

# Testing gates

The gates every landing passes, over the tests [`testing`](../SKILL.md) classifies and the
builds [`testing-builds`](../builds/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Regressions

Every batch checks, formats and lints the workspace on the tree it lands, with warnings
denied, as [`toolchain`](../../../rust/toolchain/SKILL.md) describes, and tests what its
change can affect: its module and the modules that depend on it, as `modules.json` records
them, each by its tests' module paths.

Every build of those gates runs in the raw bindings' campaign mode, as
[`bindgen`](../../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md)'s Build modes section describes, so that each fails when the
committed bindings do not match their input. A batch that changed the raw bindings, or a
landing that changes `c/`, also packages the safe crate, built alone in bundled mode from
the C it packages, with no build variant selected. Until the out-of-tree wrappers are
published, each crate the package depends on is patched to its local source, so that the
package builds alone.

The tests run against the matching variant, or a private replacement, and each event runs
them to its own depth:

- a batch: the tests above, plain and under ASan/UBSan, and its own tests under each other
  sanitizer its items call for, such as TSan where it asserts `Send` or `Sync` or adds a
  threaded callback, or MSan where C leaves memory it hands over partly unwritten;
- a wave's end, and a module's end, its switch in a port: the workspace's tests, plain,
  under every available sanitizer, under Miri and under BSan as below, less each stage's
  slow list;
- a full run: every test of the workspace under every stage, the slow lists not applied.
  It runs in the background, beside the campaign's work, by default after every fifth
  module the campaign integrates; and
- a ship point: a full run, with the coverage measurement.
<!-- TODO: a wave's end and a module's end are run by the wave's last review batch and the
module pass, so a campaign without review runs neither: they need an owner there. -->

The slow list is the campaign's skip file, which holds, per stage, the tests that take over a
minute under that stage, each by its exact name with the time measured. A test on it is
skipped at a wave's and a module's end and runs in every full run, so that the ends stay
short enough to run each time and no test goes unrun for long. A test joins the list when
an end's run measures it over the minute, and leaves when a full run measures it under. A
skip weakens a gate: the list's changes since the last ship point are put to the user at
each ship point.

BSan, when available, is run for every batch, at a wave's end and at a module's end:

- For a batch, it runs only on the individual tests or reproducers the batch expects to
  trigger it, each by exact name and alone; never on a whole test binary, a suite or the
  workspace.
- At a wave's and a module's end, it runs as a gate over the whole workspace, less its
  slow list, one invocation per test binary, as many side by side as
  [`concurrency`](../../../operations/concurrency/SKILL.md) describes, each under a `timeout`.

The slow list keeps a slow test out of the ends, not out of a full run, which a test BSan
cannot finish within that `timeout` fails every time. Such a test is sized for BSan: in the
configuration BSan's build sets, it runs fewer inputs, chosen to keep reaching every path
it checks, while every other build runs it whole.

A batch runs the tests it wrote under Miri. Miri is also run at every wave's and module's
end, as a gate over the whole workspace, less its slow list: one Miri run on the pinned
nightly per test binary, the library's and each integration suite's, as many side by side as
[`concurrency`](../../../operations/concurrency/SKILL.md) describes, each skipping the
compile-fail tests. The gate passes only
with no Miri error: a test that stops at the foreign boundary without the attribute gets
it, and any other Miri error is a UB candidate of the item it touches.

`end-gates`, beside this skill and documented by its `--help`, runs a wave's and a
module's end gates so, over a snapshot of the tree, so that work goes on in the tree while
they run: the format check and the lints with warnings denied, once per export-feature set
the batch checks, the workspace under each variant, Miri and BSan per test binary, and the
slow list's tests skipped by name, each skip checked against its binary's test list before
anything runs. A batch's own format and lint gates run the same way, over the commit it
lands, so that the result it records is that tree's.

Each gate run starts in the background and is waited on to exit; its output is neither
polled nor read while it runs. BSan reports false positives at the foreign boundary, so
only a true positive, a report that reproduces through the Rust side as a single test or
standalone reproducer, becomes a UB finding.

Every translation and review batch measures the consumer-facing API of its items against
the tip it rebased onto, each change classified as the dashboard's API stability columns
name them. An item's API is fixed by its first landing: a later landing
that changes or removes it, a port, a later stage, a rebind or a review fix alike, breaks
its consumers, and is kept only with its reason recorded in the batch's notes, such as a
soundness fix; the measure does not fail the gate. A module's integration measures every
item of the module against the module's base, and a ship point the whole crate against the
previous ship point.

When C changed, the configured C build and baseline run. A wrap-only batch with no C
change does not need the full C baseline.

A batch validates its own change on its own base first. Its rebase onto the integration
branch, under the landing lock that [`versioning`](../../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Landing section
describes, then combines that change with the work landed since: the gates run again are
those that could catch a regression the combination introduces, judged from what the
batch's change and the rebased-in changes touch and how they could interact. A gate that
neither side's changes could affect keeps the result it had, and a rebase that conflicts
makes the resolved tree new work of the batch's own.

module's export feature off, so that the ported Rust is tested beside the C it replaces.

gateway without linking it, and each export is checked at compile time against the raw
binding of the C declaration it replaces, so that a signature that drifts from C's fails
to build.

A module's switch runs as
[`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section
describes. Its gates are a module's end's, in campaign mode over the variants built from
the C that remains, and
the target's remaining C tests, which link the remaining C and the safe crate's Rust static
library, so that the C reaches the ported module through its exports: the module's tied C
tests that use only its public API among them, as the porting workflow's Tests follow
their modules section describes. Before a tied C test leaves, the cases none of the
module's `unit_pub` tests carries over are listed, as [`testing`](../SKILL.md)'s C tests

# Testing builds

The builds every test of [`testing`](../SKILL.md) runs against, and how coverage is measured
over them.

## 1. Builds

Tests run against the target's prebuilt, immutable builds, recorded as the `variants` of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`: each an out-of-tree `dir` and the `configure` and `build`
commands run from it, its `version` raised whenever a command changes. They are:

- `plain`, the functional baseline;
- `coverage`, the coverage-instrumented build for campaign measurements, instrumented as
  [Coverage](#2-coverage) describes; and
- one variant per sanitizer the campaign enables, whose tests build the Rust with the same
  LLVM sanitizer as the C, the C's clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version as for
  coverage, so that one runtime serves both and a report from the Rust's own unsafe code is
  caught too, and whose C consumers that link the safe crate's Rust static library, from a
  module's switch on, link one built with the same instrumentation:
  - `asan-ubsan`, the general build, which FFI and lifecycle tests use;
  - `msan`, which instruments every component, the standard library included;
  - `tsan`, separate from `asan-ubsan`, since ASan and TSan instrument the same memory
    operations and their runtimes conflict; and
  - `bsan`, when BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain is installed and answers its version;
    it instruments the C through its own matched clang.

A Rust- or bindgen-only change reuses a matching variant: same C revision, `build.json`
version, compiler and instrumentation. Nothing writes into a variant's `dir`: each run's
logs and outputs go to paths of its own. A change to the compiled target, or no matching
variant, needs a private build, which the raw bindings link when `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` names
it in place of a variant, and the shared variants are rebuilt once that change lands.

## 2. Coverage

Coverage is counted with one instrument for C and Rust, so that a C figure and a Rust
figure, and the campaign's figures and those of a crate it is compared with, are counted
alike, and count the code under test only:

- **Instrumentation.** The `coverage` variant compiles the C with clang's source-based
  coverage, `-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping` in its compile and link flags,
  from a clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version, and the Rust is compiled on that
  nightly with `-C instrument-coverage`. One profiling runtime counts both, into a profile
  per process and module (`LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=<dir>/%p-%m.profraw`), and the nightly's
  `llvm-profdata` and `llvm-cov` read both. gcc's coverage instrumentation and gcov are not used: their
  lines follow the line table of the optimized code, which the optimization level changes,
  so their figures cannot be compared with Rust's.
- **Test code.** Test code is not instrumented, so it is neither credited as covered nor
  counted as code to cover. Counted, it would inflate the suite that runs it, whose own
  lines run whenever it does, and deflate every other suite, whose denominator would hold
  lines it never runs. Every test item of the measured crate, under `#[test]`,
  `#[cfg(test)]` or a `cfg` that requires `test`, carries `#[coverage(off)]`, which covers
  everything nested in it, and the crate root enables `#![feature(coverage_attribute)]`.
  The attributes are added in a scratch copy of the measured tree under `crustify/tmp/`,
  which is measured in its place, so that the measured crates are not changed. Integration
  test crates, examples, benches, the crate root's build script and the generated raw
  bindings under `sys/` are left out of the report by path. Test code that is not an item, such as a `#[cfg(test)]`
  block inside a library function, stays instrumented, and is reported with the figures.
- **Objects.** C coverage is read from the objects the tests load: the variant's shared
  libraries, or the object files a crate links statically, every TU compiled into them
  counting, and one no test reaches at zero. A figure covers the sources of the library it
  names, selected by directory, so that the copies of its inline functions and of its TUs
  that other libraries compile, the configuration headers the build generates and the C's
  own tests count toward none. Rust coverage is read from every test and doctest binary of
  the crate. All objects are passed for every suite, so that every suite has the same
  denominator.
- **Suites.** Each suite runs alone, into its own profile directory, merged into one
  profile; the total merges the suites' profiles, so it is their union, never their sum.
  Doctests are a suite of their own.
- **Figures.** The figures are the totals `llvm-cov report` prints, unmodified: line,
  function and region coverage, line coverage leading. Its per-line views (`llvm-cov show`
  and the LCOV export) count lines differently, marking the bodies of C macro definitions
  as executed: they locate gaps, and never compute a figure.
- **Comparisons.** A crate the campaign is compared with is measured the same way: its
  test items marked in a scratch copy, its own release of the C built as the `coverage`
  variant is, its suites run alone, and its figures read from `llvm-cov report`. A
  comparison names its scope, and both sides are measured over the same one.

### 2.1 A worklist's coverage

A worklist's tests run against the campaign's `coverage` variant, measured as
above, and coverage is inspected for the C and Rust execution
paths belonging to the worklist. Focused tests are added to cover its reachable uncovered
paths. Paths that remain uncovered because they are unreachable, environment-dependent, or
intentionally nondeterministic are reported as such.

Coverage is maximized, not gated. Each worklist reports its regions and branches beside
its lines, and which of its types' states and transitions, as the analysis lists them, its
tests reach. In a port, a module's C is the reference until its switch: its coverage
under the module's equivalence tests shows how much of its behaviour they compare, set
against what its own C tests reach. From the switch on, the module's coverage is its
Rust's.

end, as a gate over the whole workspace, less its slow list: one Miri run on the pinned
nightly per test binary, the library's and each integration suite's, as many side by side as

compile-fail tests. The gate passes only

it, and any other Miri error is a UB candidate of the item it touches.

module's end gates so, over a snapshot of the tree, so that work goes on in the tree while

the C that remains, and

their modules section describes. Before a tied C test leaves, the cases none of the

# Testing builds

The builds every test of [`testing`](../SKILL.md) runs against, and how coverage is measured
over them.

## 1. Builds

Tests run against the target's prebuilt, immutable builds, recorded as the `variants` of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`: each an out-of-tree `dir` and the `configure` and `build`
commands run from it, its `version` raised whenever a command changes. They are:

- `plain`, the functional baseline;
- `coverage`, the coverage-instrumented build for campaign measurements, instrumented as
  [Coverage](#2-coverage) describes; and
- one variant per sanitizer the campaign enables, whose tests build the Rust with the same
  LLVM sanitizer as the C, the C's clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version as for
  coverage, so that one runtime serves both and a report from the Rust's own unsafe code is
  caught too, and whose C consumers that link the safe crate's Rust static library, from a
  module's switch on, link one built with the same instrumentation:
  - `asan-ubsan`, the general build, which FFI and lifecycle tests use;
  - `msan`, which instruments every component, the standard library included;
  - `tsan`, separate from `asan-ubsan`, since ASan and TSan instrument the same memory
    operations and their runtimes conflict; and
  - `bsan`, when BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain is installed and answers its version;
    it instruments the C through its own matched clang.

A Rust- or bindgen-only change reuses a matching variant: same C revision, `build.json`
version, compiler and instrumentation. Nothing writes into a variant's `dir`: each run's
logs and outputs go to paths of its own. A change to the compiled target, or no matching
variant, needs a private build, which the raw bindings link when `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` names
it in place of a variant, and the shared variants are rebuilt once that change lands.

## 2. Coverage

Coverage is counted with one instrument for C and Rust, so that a C figure and a Rust
figure, and the campaign's figures and those of a crate it is compared with, are counted
alike, and count the code under test only:

- **Instrumentation.** The `coverage` variant compiles the C with clang's source-based
  coverage, `-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping` in its compile and link flags,
  from a clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version, and the Rust is compiled on that
  nightly with `-C instrument-coverage`. One profiling runtime counts both, into a profile
  per process and module (`LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=<dir>/%p-%m.profraw`), and the nightly's
  `llvm-profdata` and `llvm-cov` read both. gcc's coverage instrumentation and gcov are not used: their
  lines follow the line table of the optimized code, which the optimization level changes,
  so their figures cannot be compared with Rust's.
- **Test code.** Test code is not instrumented, so it is neither credited as covered nor
  counted as code to cover. Counted, it would inflate the suite that runs it, whose own
  lines run whenever it does, and deflate every other suite, whose denominator would hold
  lines it never runs. Every test item of the measured crate, under `#[test]`,
  `#[cfg(test)]` or a `cfg` that requires `test`, carries `#[coverage(off)]`, which covers
  everything nested in it, and the crate root enables `#![feature(coverage_attribute)]`.
  The attributes are added in a scratch copy of the measured tree under `crustify/tmp/`,
  which is measured in its place, so that the measured crates are not changed. Integration
  test crates, examples, benches, the crate root's build script and the generated raw
  bindings under `sys/` are left out of the report by path. Test code that is not an item, such as a `#[cfg(test)]`
  block inside a library function, stays instrumented, and is reported with the figures.
- **Objects.** C coverage is read from the objects the tests load: the variant's shared
  libraries, or the object files a crate links statically, every TU compiled into them
  counting, and one no test reaches at zero. A figure covers the sources of the library it
  names, selected by directory, so that the copies of its inline functions and of its TUs
  that other libraries compile, the configuration headers the build generates and the C's
  own tests count toward none. Rust coverage is read from every test and doctest binary of
  the crate. All objects are passed for every suite, so that every suite has the same
  denominator.
- **Suites.** Each suite runs alone, into its own profile directory, merged into one
  profile; the total merges the suites' profiles, so it is their union, never their sum.
  Doctests are a suite of their own.
- **Figures.** The figures are the totals `llvm-cov report` prints, unmodified: line,
  function and region coverage, line coverage leading. Its per-line views (`llvm-cov show`
  and the LCOV export) count lines differently, marking the bodies of C macro definitions
  as executed: they locate gaps, and never compute a figure.
- **Comparisons.** A crate the campaign is compared with is measured the same way: its
  test items marked in a scratch copy, its own release of the C built as the `coverage`
  variant is, its suites run alone, and its figures read from `llvm-cov report`. A
  comparison names its scope, and both sides are measured over the same one.

### 2.1 A worklist's coverage

A worklist's tests run against the campaign's `coverage` variant, measured as
above, and coverage is inspected for the C and Rust execution
paths belonging to the worklist. Focused tests are added to cover its reachable uncovered
paths. Paths that remain uncovered because they are unreachable, environment-dependent, or
intentionally nondeterministic are reported as such.

Coverage is maximized, not gated. Each worklist reports its regions and branches beside
its lines, and which of its types' states and transitions, as the analysis lists them, its
tests reach. In a port, a module's C is the reference until its switch: its coverage
under the module's equivalence tests shows how much of its behaviour they compare, set
against what its own C tests reach. From the switch on, the module's coverage is its
Rust's.

name: porting-types
description: "How a scheduled C type is reimplemented in safe Rust, porting's type route: structs, unions, enums and typedefs, each with its later stages. Read before porting any type, and when reviewing ports."

# Porting types

How a scheduled C type is reimplemented in safe Rust: the type route, which follows
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section and starts from
[`binding-types`](../../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s; the symbols it reaches are
[`porting-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s.

A ported type's surface covers every field the targeted symbols touch and every lifecycle
primitive, not only those the public API publishes.

## 1. Structs

Ported storage becomes Rust-owned only once no C path accesses, allocates or frees it.
While C still owns either operation, compatible storage is retained and the blocker
reported.

A layout is ported only once no unported C of the target touches it: no field toucher,
and no other layout user. Tests and the C consumers outside the target do not count, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes, so neither a test's field access nor a definition in an installed header keeps
the layout in C. A struct whose layout another module's C still uses is wrapped where the
order places it instead, keeping its C layout behind a binding, and takes its native layout
from its `port/layout`, as [`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later
stages section schedules it.

A struct's lifecycle API is fixed by the item that first gives it a safe API, its port, or
the wrap that precedes its later stages: the owners, handles, constructors, drop and clone
its consumers use from then on, which its later stages keep. Each lifecycle routine behind
them is ported where the order places it, as a function of its own, so that a routine
whose call graph is not ported yet does not bring it forward: until then, the owner's
policy calls the C routine through its raw binding, as a binding's does. Its storage stays
in C's allocator while any C allocates or frees it raw, a lifecycle routine of its own
module still in C included, so that what Rust allocates is never freed by C's releaser,
nor the reverse.

Its handles keep the names that item gives them, `Foo`, `FooRef`, `FooMut` and its owners,
while what they name follows its later stages, so that its consumers never change, as
`binding-types`' Safe layout section describes:

- `port/layout`: the struct, wrapped until then, takes a Rust-native layout, its C layout
  gone with its last C layout user. `Foo` is defined in its module's native code, out of `ffi_import`, each field of the
  native type that keeps the ownership the analysis established, an owning string a
  `String` and a borrowed one a borrow; `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>` become aliases of
  `&'a Foo` and `&'a mut Foo`, and the getters and setters move to `impl Foo`, reading and
  writing its fields; and
- `port/memory`: its storage moves from C's allocator to Rust's: its owners become aliases
  of the native ones, `FooBox` of `Box<Foo>` and `FooArc` of `Arc<Foo>`, which allocate and
  drop it natively, with native Rust lifecycle operations instead of the C primitives.

Each switches with its own stage, or with the struct's port where that stage is not
planned, and the two stages come in either order. A `port/memory` before the struct's
`port/layout` keeps its C layout and its handles, and moves its owners to Rust's allocator
alone: they stay the C-layout owners, over a policy of Rust's allocator, since remaining
C still holds pointers into the object and reads its fields, which a native owner's claim
to sole access would break. Its `port/layout` then makes them the native ones.
A `port/layout` before the struct's `port/memory` makes its boxes and runs the standard ones
with C's allocator as their parameter, where C releases the storage with that allocator's
free alone, the native type is not zero-sized and needs no drop, and C keeps no pointer into
it; its `port/memory` then makes them `Box<Foo>` and `Vec<Foo>`. A struct that misses any of
them, or whose owner is reference-counted, has no such owner: its owner is hand-written, or
its `port/memory` comes no later than its `port/layout`.

From its native layout on, from its port or its `port/layout`, a struct has by-value
constructors, `Foo::new(…) -> Foo`, and a constructor that returns an owner builds the
value and moves it into the owner, whose allocator its stage decides: C's while
any C still frees it raw, Rust's from its `port/memory`.

While C keeps its address, as `binding-types`' Lifecycle section describes, a struct with a
native layout is `!Unpin` and its native handles are pinned: `FooMut<'a>` is an alias of
`Pin<&'a mut Foo>` and `FooBox` of `Pin<Box<Foo>>`, and an export gateway rebuilds the
pinned handle from the pointer C passes it. Once no remaining C keeps its address, the
struct becomes `Unpin`, so that its pinned handles give plain access, and its aliases keep
their `Pin`, unchanged for its consumers.

## 2. Unions

A union's safe API is the tagged Rust enum [`binding-types`](../../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s Unions
section presents it as, from its port. Its storage keeps the C union, with its
discriminator beside it, while C uses its layout, and is ported as a struct's is, with the
same later stages: its `port/layout` makes the tagged enum its storage, the discriminator
folded into the enum's tag. A union whose tag what refers to it holds becomes a tagged
enum too, once no other C uses its layout, its referrers' tags folded into it.

## 3. Enums

A ported enum takes the safe type [`binding-types`](../../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s Enums section gives
it, and its header keeps the C definition for the remaining C: the two are not linked,
beyond the Rust type's annotation, as the [conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Anchors
section describes, and the enum is not exported.

A closed enum keeps its integer form, which `binding-types`' Enums section describes, only while
remaining C uses it, its constants or values of its type. Its later stage, `port/layout`,
removes that form, its C layout: its `repr`, its discriminants and its conversions. Since
that stage leaves the safe API its consumers use as it is, as [`porting`](../SKILL.md)
requires, the conversions a port writes for an enum no wrapper gave a safe API are
crate-private: the module's unsafe regions convert through them, and no consumer does. A
closed enum that no remaining C uses by its port has no integer form, and a flags enum or
an enum without a name has no later stage. Which enums are closed is the plan's judgment,
as [`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section describes: a
port whose analysis finds otherwise gives the enum the form its analysis finds, and reports
the mismatch, which the next planner run corrects.

## 4. Typedefs

A ported typedef takes the Rust form [`binding-types`](../../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s Typedefs section
gives it, which is native from its port, and its header keeps the C typedef for the
remaining C: the two are not linked, beyond the Rust form's annotation, and the typedef is
not exported. It has no later stage: no C form of it remains in Rust for one to remove.

name: porting
description: "How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust: its native API, its later stages, the FFI boundary and its exports, and the routes porting-types and porting-symbols give types and symbols. Read before porting any item, and when reviewing ports."
---

# Porting

How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust. A port starts from the item's
analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes, and keeps C interoperability
and observable behaviour for as long as C consumes the item. A type takes the type route,
for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`porting-types`](types/SKILL.md) describes; a
symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, static inline functions
and macros, as [`porting-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

A port gives an item its native safe API at once, and that API does not change after it.
An item the remaining C still uses keeps a C form behind it, its C layout, its storage in
C's allocator, its export or its integer values, so that the C keeps working while its
Rust consumers stay agnostic of which form implements it. The later stages its kind
describes below migrate that form to Rust, part by part, once the switches that free
it have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section schedules them. An item no C uses is native in its API and its implementation from
its port.

A later stage changes the item and the code inside the crate that reaches its C form, in
its module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions
section describes, never the safe API its consumers use, and keeps the item's tests
passing. A stage that moves state out of C, a lock or a handle a type held in its C layout,
or memory C's allocator held, moves its uses onto the standard library where
[`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section lets it.

## 1. FFI boundary

`binding`'s Safe boundary section applies to a port unchanged. When a wrapper of the item
already exists, because a module that ran before needed it, the port keeps that wrapper's
safe API and replaces only what is behind it, so that its consumers do not change, as do
its later stages. A standard-library operation is used directly when it is equivalent and
no C-interoperability requirement remains, an out-of-tree library's entity included, as
`binding`'s Safe boundary section describes.

While C consumers remain, a ported item is re-exported to C as the
[conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports section describes:

- The raw gateway, its module's `ffi_export` region, reconstructs safe wrappers and calls
  the native function.
- The gateway is compiled only under its module's export feature, which stays off until
  the module switches, so that the exports never collide with the C they replace.
- At the switch, the Rust static library is linked in place of the TU through the actual
  build system, without assuming link mechanics, and the TU is deleted, as
  [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes.

description: "How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust: its native API, its later stages, the FFI boundary and its exports, and the routes porting-types and porting-symbols give types and symbols. Read before porting any item, and when reviewing ports."
---

# Porting

How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust. A port starts from the item's
analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes, and keeps C interoperability
and observable behaviour for as long as C consumes the item. A type takes the type route,
for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`porting-types`](types/SKILL.md) describes; a
symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, static inline functions
and macros, as [`porting-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

A port gives an item its native safe API at once, and that API does not change after it.
An item the remaining C still uses keeps a C form behind it, its C layout, its storage in
C's allocator, its export or its integer values, so that the C keeps working while its
Rust consumers stay agnostic of which form implements it. The later stages its kind
describes below migrate that form to Rust, part by part, once the switches that free
it have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section schedules them. An item no C uses is native in its API and its implementation from
its port.

A later stage changes the item and the code inside the crate that reaches its C form, in
its module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions
section describes, never the safe API its consumers use, and keeps the item's tests
passing. A stage that moves state out of C, a lock or a handle a type held in its C layout,
or memory C's allocator held, moves its uses onto the standard library where
[`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section lets it.

## 1. FFI boundary

`binding`'s Safe boundary section applies to a port unchanged. When a wrapper of the item
already exists, because a module that ran before needed it, the port keeps that wrapper's
safe API and replaces only what is behind it, so that its consumers do not change, as do
its later stages. A standard-library operation is used directly when it is equivalent and
no C-interoperability requirement remains, an out-of-tree library's entity included, as
`binding`'s Safe boundary section describes.

While C consumers remain, a ported item is re-exported to C as the
[conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports section describes:

- The raw gateway, its module's `ffi_export` region, reconstructs safe wrappers and calls
  the native function.
- The gateway is compiled only under its module's export feature, which stays off until
  the module switches, so that the exports never collide with the C they replace.
- At the switch, the Rust static library is linked in place of the TU through the actual
  build system, without assuming link mechanics, and the TU is deleted, as
  [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes.

name: bindgen
description: "How the raw bindings are laid out, generated, built in each mode, landed and published. Read before changing allowlists, shims, wrapper headers or build.rs, or scaffolding the bindings."
---

# Raw bindings

How a campaign's raw bindings are laid out, generated, built and shipped. They are
generated by bindgen from the C under `c/`, one module per link unit, and ship inside the
safe crate as its public `sys` module, with the C they bind: the published crate carries
the generated bindings, so that a dependent builds without bindgen or libclang, and the C
that remains, so that a dependent has the whole library and reaches what is not
translated yet through the raw bindings. How the safe crate uses them is
[`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s; their lints and formatting are
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Generated code section's.

## 1. Layout

```text
<repository>/
├── Cargo.toml            the safe crate's manifest; bindgen an optional build dependency
├── build.rs              builds or locates the C, compiles the C wrappers, regenerates on request
├── c/                    the C that remains, built into the crate
├── sys/<link-unit>/      one link unit's bindings
│   ├── wrapper.h         the headers they cover: the installed headers, and the internal headers its batches bind items of
│   ├── allowlist.txt     one `function|type|var <regex>` per line, filled by the batches
│   ├── external.txt      the types other link units' bindings own, one regex per line
│   ├── shims.h
│   ├── shims.c           the `crustify_<NAME>` macro shims
│   ├── bindings.rs       generated, committed
│   └── static_fns.c      generated wrappers of the allowlisted `static inline` functions, committed
└── src/sys.rs            the `sys` module: one public module per link unit, including its committed or regenerated bindings, or their doctest copy, and the re-exports of the types other link units own
```

Everything a build reads sits inside the crate, so that the packaged crate builds on its
own: no path leaves it, and `crustify/` is read only in campaign mode.

Within a link unit's Rust, `crate::sys::<link_unit>` is imported as `sys`, so that a raw
binding is `sys::<name>`, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Naming section spells it.
The `sys` module is public: a consumer reaches the C that is not translated yet through
it, under its C names. It takes the place of the ecosystem's `-sys` crates, and is named after them.

`c/` is the C that remains: in a wrap campaign the whole source, and in a port campaign
the fork's `main`, which each switch trims of the module it ports, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes. A build of
the crate therefore never holds both a module's C and the Rust that replaces it: the
remaining C reaches a ported module through the safe crate's exports, under their bare C
names, as the conventions' Exports section describes.

## 2. Generation

The bindings follow from the headers at the `c/` revision, the allowlists, the generator
settings below, the bindgen version, pinned exactly in `Cargo.toml`, and the LLVM pinned
below, so that generating
twice from the same input gives the same bytes. The settings are the same for every
campaign:

- the output is formatted by bindgen's own formatter (`prettyplease`), never by the
  toolchain's `rustfmt`, whose output differs between toolchains, so that a nightly build
  regenerates the bytes a stable one committed;
- enums are generated as constants (`Consts`), without the enum name as a prefix, which
  the safe types that bind them convert, as [`binding-types`](../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s Enums
  section describes;
- `Default` is derived, and layout tests are generated;
- C comments are kept as doc comments, and no doctest is collected from them, since they
  hold C: the generated modules are modules of the safe crate, which rustdoc cannot exempt
  one by one, so its doctests are collected from a copy of whichever bindings the build
  uses, committed or regenerated, whose C comments are plain comments: the build script
  writes it into `OUT_DIR`, and `src/sys.rs` includes it in their place under
  `cfg(doctest)`;
- each allowlisted `static inline` function gets a compiled wrapper, `<name>__extern`, in
  `static_fns.c`, and is bound under its own name through
  `#[link_name = "<name>__extern"]`, so that it is called as an exported function is:
  bindgen's `wrap_static_fns`;
- macro shims are bound like the functions they wrap; and
- an empty allowlist generates no item: `bindings.rs` holds only bindgen's banner, and
  `static_fns.c` stays, empty, so that every link unit has both generated files.

An internal header's declarations are generated, and the wrappers of its `static inline`
functions compiled, as the link unit's own translation units see them: with the include
dirs and preprocessor definitions the build of the C a mode links records for them, its
generated headers and its out-of-tree libraries' include dirs among them, and the source
dirs taken from the checkout's `c/`. An item whose declaration depends on a definition that
differs between the variants is generated from the `plain` variant's configuration in every
mode, so that the committed bindings are those of every variant.

A type that another link unit's bindings own is blocklisted, as `external.txt` lists it,
and re-exported from that link unit's module under its C name, so that each C type has one
Rust type across the crate. A type an out-of-tree library's wrapper publishes is
re-exported as its wrapper's safe type, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Routes section describes.

The bindings are generated for the campaign's target, the host's, as the setup workflow's
Builds section names it, the only target the crate supports: `src/sys.rs` fails to compile
on any other, naming it.

The C an out-of-tree library's wrapper bundles once its side campaign has ported part of
the library is compiled with its symbols prefixed, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Side campaigns section asks:
a generated header, force-included in every compile of that C and of its shims and
wrappers, renames each global symbol the library defines to `crustify_<library>_<name>`,
and bindgen binds each item under its C name with the prefixed symbol as its `link_name`,
so that the Rust names stay C's. The crate passes the header's path to the C builds of the
crates that depend on it through its build script's metadata, under its `links` key, and
those force-include it too, so that their C calls the same copy.

The LLVM that generates the bindings, its libclang and the clang bindgen asks for the
system include dirs, is pinned with the bindgen version: its install prefix and version, in
the workspace manifest's `[workspace.metadata.crustify]`, as `bindgen-llvm` and
`bindgen-llvm-version`. Campaign mode generates with it
whatever drives the build, a sanitizer's or Miri's cargo driver included, which may name
another libclang of its own, and fails, naming both versions, when the pinned one is
missing or reports another version. A dependent's regeneration into `OUT_DIR`, compared
with nothing, takes the LLVM its host finds.

## 3. Build modes

The build script runs in one of four modes:

| mode | when | C |
|---|---|---|
| bundled | by default, but for a wrapper whose `c/` is still its whole library | `c/`, built statically into `OUT_DIR` by the target's own build system, in the configuration of the `plain` variant |
| shared | the `shared` feature | `c/`, built as shared libraries into `OUT_DIR`, the same way |
| system | the `system` feature, and by default for a wrapper whose `c/` is still its whole library | an install, found through `<LIB>_DIR`, then `pkg-config` |
| campaign | `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT` names a variant, or `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` a private build | the variant's build, recorded in `crustify/artifacts/build.json`: its static archive, when it records one, else its shared libraries |

The campaign's repository sets `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT` to `plain` in its
`.cargo/config.toml`, so that every build there runs in campaign mode unless the variable
names another variant, or is set empty to build as a dependent would.

In every mode, `shims.c` and `static_fns.c` are compiled against the headers the bindings
match, with the instrumentation of the C they link, and the bindings are the committed
ones unless the `bindgen` feature regenerates them into `OUT_DIR` from the headers of that
C. Campaign mode's tests and gates always regenerate them.

Bundled mode links the C statically, so that the bindings and the C they call always come
from the same revision; it sets no rpath. It builds `c/` against the out-of-tree libraries
its configuration uses as the target's build system finds them on the building host; a
dependent whose host lacks one supplies it through that build system's own search paths,
such as `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` and `PKG_CONFIG_PATH`. Shared mode leaves the remaining C's references
to ported modules undefined in its shared libraries, and the build script has the final
binary export what resolves them (`-Wl,--export-dynamic-symbol=<name>` for each export),
as a cdylib already does; the libraries are found beside the binary, through an `$ORIGIN`
rpath, and ship with it.

System mode serves a crate whose `c/` is still the whole source: once a port campaign has
switched a module, an install of the library would hold that module's C beside the Rust
that replaces it, and the build fails, naming the switched modules. It checks the
version: the library found must be the one the bindings were generated from, as its build
system reports it (`pkg-config --modversion`), or, for an out-of-tree library's wrapper, a
release ABI-compatible with it, which shares its soname. Another version fails the build
with both versions named, unless the `bindgen` feature regenerates the bindings for it. Each link
unit's module exports the version the bindings match as `C_VERSION`. `<LIB>_DIR` names an
install prefix: the build reads the headers under its `include/`, links the library under
its `lib/`, and takes the version from `lib/pkgconfig/<lib>.pc`. Without it, `pkg-config`
finds the library, which is linked as `pkg-config` resolves it, with no rpath.

An install carries neither the internal headers nor the functions its shared library does
not export, whichever header declares them, public or internal, and the shared libraries
shared mode builds lack the same functions, since the target's own configuration builds
them. Once the bindings reach either, system mode cannot serve the crate, nor shared mode
once they reach a function a shared library hides: the build fails in each, naming what
the library lacks, as system mode fails for a switched module, and bundled mode, whose
build in `OUT_DIR` has both, becomes the crate's default. The `bindgen` feature then regenerates from that build's
headers, never from an install's.

A link unit the target links as an executable, such as a command-line tool, has no
library. Bundled mode compiles its translation units as the target's build system records
them, without linking the executable, archives their objects and links the archive;
campaign mode links them from the variant's static archive, which holds them, as
[`setup`](../../workflows/setup/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes; shared and system
modes, which link libraries, refuse its feature, naming the modes that serve it. An archive
member is linked only where one of its symbols is referenced, so a test that references
the translation unit defining the executable's `main`, directly or through another member
that references it, links a second `main` beside its harness's and fails to link. That
unit's other symbols are therefore ported to exports first, so that the members which
reference them stop pulling it in, and until then the units that pull it in are tested
through the variant's executable, run as a child process.

Campaign mode serves the campaign while it extends the bindings: batches add allowlist
entries and shims, and the bindings follow from them. It needs bindgen, which the safe
crate enables for its own tests through a dev-dependency on itself with the `bindgen`
feature, so that the campaign's tests and gates regenerate while dependents build from
the committed bindings. A build that does not enable the feature, such as the crate's
documentation, uses the committed bindings unchecked; the tests and gates always enable it.
The bindings it generates are compared with the committed ones: a difference fails the
build, naming the regenerated file, unless `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE` is set, in which case
they are written over `bindings.rs` and `static_fns.c`. It links the C the variant built,
so that every test runs against the instrumented C it was built for. A variant that
records a `static` archive, as [`setup`](../../workflows/setup/SKILL.md)'s Builds section
describes, has it linked statically, with the libraries its shared library links, so that
the Rust reaches the internal functions the shared library does not export, and the
remaining C resolves the exports within the same link, as bundled mode's does; only the
out-of-tree libraries' installs of the same variant take an rpath. A variant that records
none has its shared libraries linked with an rpath to them, and the test binaries export
what the remaining C resolves to, as shared mode does.

No build links two copies of a module: a mode links either a module's C or the Rust that
replaces it, never both, and the Rust static library that the target's remaining C links
from a module's switch on carries no C of its own, as the porting workflow's Builds
section describes.

## 4. Extending

The bindings grow with the batches: a batch whose items need a raw binding the bindings
lack extends its own link unit's input, and nothing else:

1. its link unit's `allowlist.txt` gains only the FFI items its items need, and
   `wrapper.h` an internal header only when one of them is declared there;
2. a shim is added to `shims.h` and `shims.c` only for a macro whose expansion depends on
   the build's configuration, as `crustify_<NAME>`, as
   [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section describes;
3. the bindings are regenerated, in campaign mode with `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE` set; and
4. the safe crate is built and tested against them.

Where its link unit's headers name a type another link unit owns, the batch also extends
what the re-export needs, and only that: the type joins its own link unit's `external.txt`,
the owning link unit's `allowlist.txt` too while its bindings lack the type, and the link
unit's module in `src/sys.rs` re-exports it from the owner's, under its C name.

An allowlist or `wrapper.h` change alone leaves the C library as it is, so it reuses a
prebuilt variant; a shim compiles with the crate, as [Build modes](#3-build-modes) describes.

## 5. Landing

A batch that changes an allowlist, `external.txt`, a shim or `wrapper.h` regenerates the
bindings and commits them in the same landing, so that the committed bindings always match
their input. The gates that check it, and that the crate packages, are
[`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section's.

## 6. Publishing

The safe crate is published with its raw bindings and the C it bundles. The packaged crate
holds the layout above, `src/`, the files of `c/` that the bundled build reads and the
C's license files, and nothing else of the repository but its README and the files the
package manager adds to every package, such as its manifest's original and its lockfile.

campaign mode links them from the variant's static archive, which holds them, as
[`setup`](../../workflows/setup/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes; shared and system
modes, which link libraries, refuse its feature, naming the modes that serve it. An archive
member is linked only where one of its symbols is referenced, so a test that references
the translation unit defining the executable's `main`, directly or through another member
that references it, links a second `main` beside its harness's and fails to link. That
unit's other symbols are therefore ported to exports first, so that the members which
reference them stop pulling it in, and until then the units that pull it in are tested
through the variant's executable, run as a child process.

Campaign mode serves the campaign while it extends the bindings: batches add allowlist
entries and shims, and the bindings follow from them. It needs bindgen, which the safe
crate enables for its own tests through a dev-dependency on itself with the `bindgen`
feature, so that the campaign's tests and gates regenerate while dependents build from
the committed bindings. A build that does not enable the feature, such as the crate's
documentation, uses the committed bindings unchecked; the tests and gates always enable it.
The bindings it generates are compared with the committed ones: a difference fails the
build, naming the regenerated file, unless `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE` is set, in which case
they are written over `bindings.rs` and `static_fns.c`. It links the C the variant built,
so that every test runs against the instrumented C it was built for. A variant that
records a `static` archive, as [`setup`](../../workflows/setup/SKILL.md)'s Builds section
describes, has it linked statically, with the libraries its shared library links, so that
the Rust reaches the internal functions the shared library does not export, and the
remaining C resolves the exports within the same link, as bundled mode's does; only the
out-of-tree libraries' installs of the same variant take an rpath. A variant that records
none has its shared libraries linked with an rpath to them, and the test binaries export
what the remaining C resolves to, as shared mode does.

No build links two copies of a module: a mode links either a module's C or the Rust that
replaces it, never both, and the Rust static library that the target's remaining C links
from a module's switch on carries no C of its own, as the porting workflow's Builds
section describes.

## 4. Extending

The bindings grow with the batches: a batch whose items need a raw binding the bindings
lack extends its own link unit's input, and nothing else:

1. its link unit's `allowlist.txt` gains only the FFI items its items need, and
   `wrapper.h` an internal header only when one of them is declared there;
2. a shim is added to `shims.h` and `shims.c` only for a macro whose expansion depends on
   the build's configuration, as `crustify_<NAME>`, as
   [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section describes;
3. the bindings are regenerated, in campaign mode with `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE` set; and
4. the safe crate is built and tested against them.

Where its link unit's headers name a type another link unit owns, the batch also extends
what the re-export needs, and only that: the type joins its own link unit's `external.txt`,
the owning link unit's `allowlist.txt` too while its bindings lack the type, and the link
unit's module in `src/sys.rs` re-exports it from the owner's, under its C name.

An allowlist or `wrapper.h` change alone leaves the C library as it is, so it reuses a
prebuilt variant; a shim compiles with the crate, as [Build modes](#3-build-modes) describes.

## 5. Landing

A batch that changes an allowlist, `external.txt`, a shim or `wrapper.h` regenerates the
bindings and commits them in the same landing, so that the committed bindings always match
their input. The gates that check it, and that the crate packages, are
[`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section's.

## 6. Publishing

The safe crate is published with its raw bindings and the C it bundles. The packaged crate
holds the layout above, `src/`, the files of `c/` that the bundled build reads and the
C's license files, and nothing else of the repository but its README and the files the
package manager adds to every package, such as its manifest's original and its lockfile.

What the code is named and where it sits is [`conventions`](../conventions/SKILL.md)'s; these are the rules the toolchain enforces on it. ## 1. Toolchains The workspace builds and tests on stable Rust, pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml` to the stable release current when the repository is created, with the `clippy` and `rustfmt` components. Miri, the sanitizer and coverage instrumentation of the Rust, BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain aside, and the formatter's unstable options need nightly: a nightly pinned by date, recorded in the workspace manifest as `[workspace.metadata.crustify] nightly = "nightly-"`, and named explicitly wherever it runs. A toolchain is moved forward only between waves, in a commit of its own. ## 2. Edition and manifests Every crate uses Rust edition 2024, with the workspace's `rust-version` set to the pinned stable release. The shared package fields (`edition`, `rust-version`, `license`, `repository`) are declared once, in `[workspace.package]`, and inherited. Every crate inherits the workspace's lints with `[lints] workspace = true`. ## 3. Lints The workspace declares its lints in `[workspace.lints.rust]` and `[workspace.lints.clippy]`. Every gate runs with warnings denied, so a lint at `warn` fails a landing as surely as one at `deny`; `deny` marks the lints no item may opt out of. ### 3.1 rustc | lint | level | why | |---|---|---| | `nonstandard_style` (`non_snake_case`, `non_camel_case_types`, `non_upper_case_globals`) | `deny` | the naming the conventions' Naming section gives: `snake_case` functions, methods, modules and variables, `UpperCamelCase` types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` constants and statics | | `unsafe_code` | `warn` | unsafe code only in a module's unsafe regions, which take it back, as [Unsafe code](#5-unsafe-code) describes | | `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` | `deny` | each unsafe operation in an `unsafe fn` sits in its own justified `unsafe` block | | `missing_docs` | `warn` | every public item carries its anchor, which is a doc comment | | `rust_2018_idioms` | `warn` | elided lifetimes in paths and other pre-2018 idioms | | `unreachable_pub`, `unused_qualifications`, `unused_lifetimes`, `let_underscore_drop`, `trivial_casts`, `trivial_numeric_casts` | `warn` | visibility the crate does not need, and casts and drops that hide intent at the foreign boundary | ### 3.2 Clippy | lints | level | why | |---|---|---| | `clippy::correctness` | `deny` | code that is outright wrong | | `clippy::all` (`suspicious`, `style`, `complexity`, `perf`), `clippy::pedantic`, `clippy::cargo` | `warn` | as much of Clippy's stable guidance as applies; `nursery` is left out, its lints still being unsettled | | `undocumented_unsafe_blocks`, `multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block`, `missing_safety_doc`, `unnecessary_safety_comment`, `unnecessary_safety_doc` | `deny` | every `unsafe` block is one justified operation, and every safety comment and `# Safety` section is where it belongs | | `mem_forget`, `allow_attributes`, `allow_attributes_without_reason` | `deny` | no leak by `mem::forget`, and every exception an `#[expect]` with a reason | | `module_inception` | `allow` | a C directory often holds a TU of its own name, so the mirrored tree nests a module in one of its name | | `module_name_repetitions` | `allow` | items keep their C-derived names where their module, mirrored from the C path, repeats them | | `multiple_crate_versions` | `allow` | the dependency graph is not the campaign's to dedupe | An item that needs an exception takes it locally, as `#[expect(, reason = "")]`, never as a crate-wide `allow`: the expectation fails once the exception is no longer needed. ### 3.3 Generated code The raw bindings' bindgen output follows C's names and shapes, so it is exempt from the workspace's lints: `src/sys.rs` allows every lint and lint group the workspace sets over each generated module, under one `#[expect(clippy::allow_attributes, reason = "…")]` naming the generated code, and the formatter skips the generated modules. The hand-written parts of the raw bindings, such as `build.rs`, `src/sys.rs` itself and the macro shims, follow the rest of this spec. ## 4. Formatting Every crate is formatted by `rustfmt`, configured once in the workspace's `rustfmt.toml`: | option | value | |---|---| | `edition`, `style_edition` | `"2024"` | | `max_width`, `comment_width` | `100` | | `newline_style` | `"Unix"` | | `use_field_init_shorthand`, `use_try_shorthand` | `true` | | `imports_granularity` | `"Module"` | | `group_imports` | `"StdExternalCrate"` | | `wrap_comments`, `normalize_comments`, `normalize_doc_attributes` | `true` | | `format_code_in_doc_comments`, `format_macro_matchers` | `true` | | `hex_literal_case` | `"Upper"` | | `reorder_impl_items` | `true` | The options from `imports_granularity` down are unstable, so the formatter runs on the pinned nightly. A landing's tree is formatted, and the gate checks that it is. ## 5. Unsafe code Every unsafe block carries a specific, falsifiable `// SAFETY:` comment: the invariant the operation relies on, and why it holds on every path that reaches it. Native Rust APIs are safe unless their caller obligation cannot be expressed in the type system; an `unsafe fn` documents that obligation in its `# Safety` section. Unsafe code sits only in a module's unsafe regions and in the raw bindings, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions section describes. A region that holds unsafe code of its own takes `unsafe_code` back where it is declared, as `#[expect(unsafe_code, reason = "")] mod ffi_import { … }`, so that the expectation fails once the region holds none; and so does each test suite and unit-test module that holds unsafe code. A region whose only unsafe code a macro of another crate expands takes none: the lint does not see that code, and the expectation would fail. A module with no region carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, which no item within it can take back. --- name: ffibox description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one." --- # ffibox ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a value; what C does not alias is plain Rust. Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md` describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes. What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there. ## Planning ### Dependencies › Adopted crates A candidate crate's soundness is read against the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists, each of which ffibox excludes from the campaign's own bindings: the crate qualifies where its safe API excludes them too, by whatever means it uses. ## Binding workflow ### Binding workflow › Rust tree The workspace depends on ffibox by path, on the checkout the host provides, which is on the campaign's working branch of it, `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }` in Crustify's image, so that each run records its revision among its task's `revisions`. The path is the checkout's canonical one, with no symbolic link on it, and a `[patch]` that redirects another source of ffibox names the same: compile-fail snapshots normalize a path dependency only where the compiler's paths match the dependency's canonical directory. ## Binding and porting Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`, `docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too. ### Binding types A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them. ### Binding types › Safe layout While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox;`, and `CArc` for `FooArc`. A value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal`. ### Binding symbols › Functions A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them. ### Binding symbols › Function pointers A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier, `callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body. A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a `CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as `docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table. ### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C. ### Porting › FFI boundary An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does with the Rust it reaches: - the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`, `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return its owners and handles; - memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C frees it through an exported release; - a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a `CPayload`; and - the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`. ### Porting types › Structs Until a ported struct's `port/layout`, its handles are ffibox's, as [Binding types › Safe layout](#binding-types--safe-layout) describes; from it on, `FooRef` and `FooMut` are aliases of native borrows. Its owners stay ffibox's until its `port/memory`, or until its `port/layout` where that comes first, as below, their policy calling its lifecycle routines, C's through their raw bindings until each is ported, then the Rust ones. A `port/memory` before its `port/layout` keeps them ffibox's and changes their policy to `RustAlloc` alone: `FooBox` becomes `CBox`, its handles unchanged, until its `port/layout` makes it `Box`, or `Pin>` while C keeps its address. Between a struct's `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, its layout is native while C still allocates or frees its storage, and ffibox's single-object owners, which hold only C-layout types, cannot hold it. Where C releases it with its allocation family's free alone, and the native type is not zero-sized and needs no drop (`size_of::() != 0` and `!core::mem::needs_drop::()`, both asserted at compile time), and C does not keep its address, `FooBox` is `Box>` and a counted run of them `Vec>`, `P` the family's `Copy` policy with the alignment the family guarantees: an existing `CLenAlloc` policy of the family, or one declared with `impl_clenalloc!`'s `align =`. A box is built with `CAllocator::try_box`, which refuses an over-aligned type at compile time and returns C's out-of-memory failure, and handed to C with `Box::into_raw_with_allocator`; a run grows with `Vec::try_reserve`, keeping C's out-of-memory failure, and is handed to C through `CVec::try_from` and `into_raw_parts`. A pointer C hands back is adopted with `Box::from_raw_in`, under the conditions `CBox::into_box`'s documentation lists, and a run with `Vec::from_raw_parts_in`, its length as its capacity, under the allocator's fit rule. Its `port/memory` makes them `Box` and `Vec`. ## Testing ### Testing › UB tests The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test. ## Reviewing Reviewing reads `docs/goals.md`. ### Reviewing › Objectives A workset's use of ffibox's primitives is reviewed against ffibox's documentation, and its hand-written representations against the contract ffibox would have enforced. Under `ub`, the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists are the checklist: each is excluded by the primitive or the producer's contract it names, or is a finding. ### Reviewing-reports › Reports A soundness or ergonomics gap in ffibox itself, in its safe primitives or its unsafe FFI seams, is a defect in a tool: a proposal, as any tool defect is. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C. ### Porting › FFI boundary An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does with the Rust it reaches: - the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`, `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return its owners and handles; - memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C frees it through an exported release; - a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a `CPayload`; and - the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`. ### Porting types › Structs Until a ported struct's `port/layout`, its handles are ffibox's, as [Binding types › Safe layout](#binding-types--safe-layout) describes; from it on, `FooRef` and `FooMut` are aliases of native borrows. Its owners stay ffibox's until its `port/memory`, or until its `port/layout` where that comes first, as below, their policy calling its lifecycle routines, C's through their raw bindings until each is ported, then the Rust ones. A `port/memory` before its `port/layout` keeps them ffibox's and changes their policy to `RustAlloc` alone: `FooBox` becomes `CBox`, its handles unchanged, until its `port/layout` makes it `Box`, or `Pin>` while C keeps its address.
